Meaning 1 — To have enough money to buy or pay for something

This is the meaning most people know first. When you can afford something, you have enough money for it. When you can't afford it, you don't.

"I want to buy a new phone, but I can't afford it right now."
"She earns a good salary, so she can afford to travel every year."
"Can you afford this apartment? The rent is very high."

Important grammar note: In this meaning, "afford" is almost always used with can or can't (or could / couldn't). You will almost never see it without one of these helpers.

The thing you're buying can be a noun:

"We can't afford a car."

Or it can be an action (verb):

"We can't afford to buy a car." (to + verb)
Meaning 2 — To be in a position where something is safe, acceptable, or possible — without necessarily involving money

This is a very important meaning that many learners miss. Here, "afford" is about consequences, not money. If you can't afford to do something, it means doing it would be too risky, too costly, or too damaging — even if no money is involved.

Think of it this way: you are in a situation where the price of making a mistake is too high — even if that price is your reputation, your health, your time, your relationship, or your chance of success.

"I can't afford to make any more mistakes. My boss is already unhappy with me."

(Making a mistake would have serious consequences for me.)

"We can't afford to waste time. The deadline is tomorrow."

(Wasting time would hurt us too much.)

"He's already behind in school. He can't afford to miss any more classes."

(The consequences of missing class would be too serious for him.)

"A doctor can't afford to be careless."

(Being careless would have unacceptable consequences.)

Notice that in all these examples, no money is involved. The logic is the same as Meaning 1 — you don't have enough "room" or "safety" to do something — but instead of money, what you're short on is the ability to handle the consequences.

The same grammar rule applies here too: almost always used with can/can't or could/couldn't, followed by a noun or to + verb.
Meaning 3 — To provide, give, or offer something (formal)

This is a more formal and literary meaning. Here, a person or a thing gives / provides something to someone. The subject is often a place, a law, an opportunity, a situation, or a thing — not just a person.

"The balcony affords a beautiful view of the mountains."

(The balcony gives / provides a beautiful view.)

"This job affords me a good income and a lot of flexibility."

(This job gives/provides me a good income and flexibility.)

"The new law affords greater protection to workers."

(The new law provides greater protection.)

"Living abroad afforded her the opportunity to learn a new language."

(Living abroad gave her / provided her the opportunity.)

Key difference from meanings 1 and 2: In this meaning, you do not need "can" or "can't." The verb works on its own, like any regular verb. Also, the subject is often a thing (a law, a place, a situation), not just a person.

This meaning is less common in everyday casual conversation, but you'll see it often in writing, news, formal speech, and literature.
How the three meanings connect — the deeper logic

All three meanings share a single underlying idea: something makes something else possible or available.

  • In Meaning 1, your money makes a purchase possible (or impossible).
  • In Meaning 2, your situation or safety margin makes an action possible (or impossible).
  • In Meaning 3, a person or thing actively provides/gives something to someone.

Once you see this common thread, the word becomes much more intuitive.

1. "Afford" implies a kind of "cost."
Even in Meaning 3, there's a quiet sense that something is being "provided" because the giver has the capacity to do so. A balcony that "affords a view" gives that view because of what it is and where it is.

2. "Can't afford to" is very common in warnings and serious statements.
When someone says "We can't afford to ignore this problem," they mean the consequences of ignoring it are too serious. This is Meaning 2, and it's everywhere in news, speeches, and serious discussions.

3. "Afford" is slightly formal even in everyday use.
You wouldn't normally say "The wall affords shade" in casual conversation — you'd say "The wall gives shade." But in writing or slightly formal speech, Meaning 3 sounds perfectly natural.
